In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

Your paper profiling the large diversity of chick retinal neurons taking advantage of single-cell mRNA sequencing is novel and exciting and this dataset published in eLife will be an important resource for retina scientists. Furthermore, the comparison with the mouse retina is of great interest and the variation among the retinal ganglion cells might represent a fundamental process by which species adapt to their visual environment.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Single cell profiling identifies 136 cell types in the chick retina" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Tom Baden (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, we are asking editors to accept without delay manuscripts, like yours, that they judge can stand as eLife papers without additional data, even if they feel that they would make the manuscript stronger. Thus the revisions requested below only address clarity and presentation.

The three reviewers found your paper novel and exciting and they are anxious to see it published in eLife as this will be an important resource for the field. Furthermore, the comparison with the mouse retina is of great interest and the variation among the retinal ganglion cells might represent a fundamental process by which species adapt to their visual environment.

However, there are a few points that you will need to address before the paper can be published, most of which should only require editorial work or bioinformatic processing.

– Present a much better description of the technical processing the scRNA seq data.

– Address the question of cell type: All reviewers feel that you have not demonstrated that you have identified 136 cell types as several could be cell states. One way to address this would be to add a pseudotime analysis to make sure that the “cell types” are not different cell states.

– The cell types that differ between species might be due to the very different stages of development of the various retinas. Showing a UMAP of all ages aggregated together would address this point.

– You should also fix the referencing to other papers that appears to be lacking.

We will be expecting a revised version soon and the field will then be able to enjoy these results.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript "Single cell profiling identifies 136 cell types in the chick retina" by Yamagata and colleagues represents a new transcriptomic atlas of the chicken retina. It explores the diversity of cell types in the avian retina, describing the functional significance of this vast diversity in terms of cell morphology, connections and spatial organization within the retina. Using a CRISPR-based assay, they show the position of the various cell types and their corresponding morphologies. Finally, the authors describe the regionalization of specific populations of glial cells in their respective identities. Overall this manuscript is an extensive documentation combining in silico exploration with in vivo validations. It is an impressive resource that will be extremely valuable to the field. While the experimental design of the study is correct and in general the data appears technically rigorous, the Results section lacks clarity in the way the data are presented, and more importantly, it does not provide sufficient information on the methods and the parameters used for the single-cell analysis. Altogether their findings appear convincing and provide an impressive resource on which the community will be able to generate new hypotheses in the field.

1) The central point that is made by the authors regards the number of cell types in the avian retina. Based on previous reports in other species, this number may be expected. But how much of the diversity one can observe in amacrine and bipolar cells is related to the transitional states of the same cell type? Also, the authors mention 10 clearly immature clusters: could these correspond to CMZ-derived or CMZ cells? Finally, even if the retina at E18 is histologically mature, some of the cells in mature clusters may be closer to full maturation than others, in particular when it comes to synapse refinement and pruning. Was this taken into account? A first step into this investigation would be to rank the cells with pseudotime alignment method (such as Monocle).

2) To what extent is the number of cell types related to i) the number of single-cells sequenced (have you controlled whether you are close to saturation?) ii) the stages used to evaluate them (E12-E18) and iii) the clustering technique (this latter was difficult to assess due to insufficient description) ?

3) Why is there no dimensionality reduction visualization of the main dataset? We see these cells aggregated with other species only in Figure 10, but nowhere can we appreciate the distinction between the main classes. Thus, it is hard to assess to what extent these classes are distinct.

4) The manuscript, presented as a resource, occasionally lacks clarity in its presentation, especially in the first pages of the Results section (Figures 1 and 2).

5) The main concern is the lack of detail in the Materials and methods section, in particular on the single-cell analysis (QCs, etc). The clustering appears to be correct, but it would be valuable to add how filtering and hierarchical clustering were performed. Also, a clarification of the rationale for the maximisation procedure used to distinguish cell types would be useful. Same for the thresholds used.

6) Regarding the data availability, the link provided does not work:

"https://singlecell.broadinstitute.org/single_cell/study/SCP1159"

7) The Introduction and Discussion are well written but poorly referenced, especially when it comes to the multi-species comparison. As this study adds to an increasing body of work on single-cell retina, it seems important to refer to the previous work (unless the number of references is limited?).

Reviewer #2:

In their manuscript "Single cell profiling identifies 136 cell types in the chick retina", Yamagata, Yan and Sanes present the first transcriptomic atlas of an avian retina. The manuscript delivers pretty much what it says on the tin: a (probably almost) complete parts-list of the chicken retina, with 6 photoreceptor types, 4 HCs, >20 BCs, >40 RGCs and close to 60 ACs – alongside Muller glia. Each of these comes with a hit-list of molecular markers than could be used to genetically target them in the future, and some are in fact confirmed in the study using their novel eCHIKIN approach.

Beyond this, the authors also compare their results from chicken to their previous results from mouse as well as species of primate including humans and find interesting links between cell classes and types. Overall, their results confirm several long-held notions, for example that avian retinas are among the more complex ones out there, that retinal cell homology works incredibly well on the retinal input side (especially HCs seem to be amazingly conserved!), while this works less well on the RGC side – possibly hinting that evolution will more readily tweak the retinal output than the input?

Finally, the work is technically excellent, the manuscript is written clearly and succinctly, and referencing is adequate.

Overall, there is a lot to like, and really nothing to dislike. As a lab that is actively investigating vision in chicks (and other species), I can attest first-hand that this dataset is incredibly useful and interesting, and I enthusiastically support publication in eLife.

Reviewer #3:

In this descriptive study the authors use scRNA-Seq to profile ~40,000 cells from the embryonic chick retina and compare them to similar datasets generated from mouse, human, and macaque. As the authors point out, the chick retina is a long-used model for retinal development and recently another paper described scRNA-Seq on the chick retina in the context of multi-species functional studies of retinal regeneration (Hoang et al., 2020). An additional study (Tegla et al., 2020) also performed scRNA-Seq of the chick retina to probe the function of developmental transcriptional programs. The field does not however have a well-documented single cell atlas of the chick retina. This current study represents such a resource that will be an important reference for the field moving forward.

1) Throughout the paper the authors associate the concept of single-cell cluster with the concept of cell type. Given that the number and size of clusters can be dynamically changed depending on analysis parameters, I would strongly recommend that the authors avoid using the term "cell type", except where this is well supported experimentally (e.g. by demonstration of a cell-mosaic arrangement of marker expression). This term is especially misleading in the title, which might more accurately be "a single cell atlas of the developing chick retina".

2) The description of the scRNA-seq analyses is really insufficient to permit replication or in some cases interpretation of the data. The authors need to give more details with regard to the specific parameters used for each analysis.

3) The authors should provide additional evidence that comparing cell classes and types between the embryonic chick retina to that of the more mature mammalian retinas is experimentally justified. Could it be that they are seeing a greater diversity of cell types in the chick retina because they are considering a greater diversity of transitional states? These multi-species comparisons would be greatly strengthened by addition of a dataset from the mature chicken retina.

claims.claim: Of the E18 retinal cells profiled, 620 were RGCs, representing approximately 2% of the total.
claims.source: Of the E18 retinal cells profiled, 620 were RGCs (Figure 1F). This fraction (~2%) was similar to that observed in other species (Macosko et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2019) but was insufficient for extensive classification of what we anticipated would be a highly heterogeneous class.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by citation to other species.

claims.claim: Magnetic beads coated with antibodies to the pan-RGC cell surface marker Thy1 were used to enrich RGCs from E16 retina before scRNA-seq.
claims.source: We therefore used magnetic beads coated with antibodies to the pan-RGC cell surface marker Thy1 (French and Jeffrey, 1986; Yamagata et al., 2002) to enrich RGCs from E16 retina before scRNA-seq.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: 9159 single-cell transcriptomes were obtained from E16 retina, of which 8107 (89%) were RGCs.
claims.source: We obtained 9159 single-cell transcriptomes, of which 8107 (89%) were RGCs (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that were used for subsequent analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1G.

claims.claim: A total of 150 clusters were obtained by reclustering each cell class separately.
claims.source: To resolve cell types within these classes, we reclustered each one separately, and obtained a total of 150 clusters (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Each cluster presumably corresponded to a cell type, a small group of closely related types, a positional variant or a developmental intermediate.
claims.source: Each presumably corresponded to a cell type, a small group of closely related types, a positional variant or, since we profiled embryonic cells, a developmental intermediate.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the clustering results.

claims.claim: eCHIKIN (electroporation- and CRISPR-mediated Homology-Instructed Knock-IN) was developed to insert fluorescent reporters into genes expressed by specific cell types.
claims.source: We call the method eCHIKIN for electroporation- and CRISPR-mediated Homology-Instructed Knock-IN.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section describing the method development.

claims.claim: eCHIKIN uses in ovo electroporation to deliver a mixture consisting of guide RNAs, Cas9 protein, and a single-strand DNA containing a reporter sequence flanked by ~70 bases gene-specific homology arms.
claims.source: We used in ovo electroporation to deliver a mixture consisting of guide RNAs, Cas9 protein, and a single-strand DNA containing a reporter sequence flanked by ~70 bases gene-specific homology arms (Gurumurthy et al., 2019; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: VSX2-HA-tagged cells were restricted to the outer part of the INL, as appropriate for BCs, and were VSX2-positive and TFAP2A-negative.
claims.source: VSX2-HA-tagged cells were restricted in the outer part of the INL, as appropriate for BCs, and were VSX2-positive and TFAP2A-negative (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B-D showing immunostaining results.

claims.claim: TFAP2A-GFP cells were present in the inner portion of the INL as appropriate for TFAP2A-expressing ACs.
claims.source: TFAP2A-GFP cells were present in the inner portion of the INL as appropriate for TFAP2A-expressing ACs (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2E.

claims.claim: RBPMS2-HA-tagged cells were confined to the ganglion cell layer, as appropriate for RGCs.
claims.source: Likewise, RBPMS2-HA-tagged cells were confined to the ganglion cell layer, as appropriate for RGCs (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Chicks are tetrachromatic, with cone types that express red opsin (OPN1LW), green opsin (OPN1MSW), blue opsin (OPN2SW), or violet opsin (OPN1SW).
claims.source: Chicks are tetrachromatic, with cone types that express red opsin (OPN1LW), green opsin (OPN1MSW), blue opsin (OPN2SW), or violet opsin (OPN1SW) (Kram et al., 2010; Enright et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Chick retina contains rods that express rhodopsin (RHO) and OPN1LW-expressing 'double-cones' (DCs) composed of tightly apposed principal and accessory cells.
claims.source: In addition to these conventional 'single-cones' (SCs), the retina also contains rods that express rhodopsin (RHO) and OPN1LW-expressing 'double-cones' (DCs) composed of tightly apposed principal and accessory cells, which together comprise about half of all PRs (Smith et al., 1985; López-López et al., 2008; Oishi et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Reclustering of PRs revealed 12 clusters, including one each expressing RHO, OPN1MSW, OPN2SW, and OPN1SW, marking them as rods and green, blue, and violet SCs, respectively.
claims.source: Reclustering of PRs revealed 12 clusters (numbered in order of descending abundance; Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), including one each expressing RHO, OPN1MSW, OPN2SW, and OPN1SW (PR clusters 3, 5, 8, and 11), marking them as rods and green, blue, and violet SCs, respectively (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Expression of OPN1LW was detected in four clusters (PR clusters 1, 2, 4, and 7), representing red SCs and DCs.
claims.source: Expression of OPN1LW was detected in four clusters (PR clusters 1, 2, 4, and 7; Figure 3B), representing red SCs and DCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3B.

claims.claim: PR7 is identified as red SCs and PR1, 2, and 4 as components of DCs.
claims.source: Thus, we identify PR7 as red SCs and PR1, 2, and 4 as components of DCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the analysis.

claims.claim: Four PR clusters expressed the PR fate determination gene PRDM1 but did not express opsins, suggesting that they were immature PRs.
claims.source: The third clade of PRs, comprising four clusters, expressed the PR fate determination gene, PRDM1 (Katoh et al., 2010; Brzezinski et al., 2013), but did not express opsins, suggesting that they were immature PRs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: At E12, ARHGAP18 was expressed by PRs in the ONL, but OPN1LW was not detectable.
claims.source: At E12, ARHGAP18 was expressed by PRs in the ONL, but OPN1LW was not detectable.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section describing in situ hybridization results.

claims.claim: At E20, OPN1LW was expressed but ARGHAP18 was not.
claims.source: Conversely, OPN1LW was expressed at E20 but ARGHAP18 was not (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D), suggesting that ARGHAP18 is transiently expressed in the ONL during development.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claims.claim: At E16, ARHGAP18 and SLIT1 were expressed by ONL cells selectively in peripheral retina, whereas OPN1LW and STRA6 were expressed by ONL cells in central retina.
claims.source: At E16, consistent with the fact that retinal differentiation proceeds in a central-to-peripheral gradient (Kahn, 1974; Spence and Robson, 1989; Prada et al., 1991; Bruhn and Cepko, 1996), ARHGAP18 and SLIT1 were expressed by ONL cells selectively in peripheral retina, whereas OPN1LW and STRA6 were by ONL cells in central retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–Q).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–Q.

claims.claim: Clustering of E18 HCs yielded five clusters, HC1-5, all expressing the canonical HC marker ONECUT3.
claims.source: Clustering of E18 HCs yielded five clusters, HC1-5 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), all expressing the canonical HC marker ONECUT3.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A.

claims.claim: LHX1 and ISL1 were detected in exclusive HC populations.
claims.source: LHX1 and ISL1 were detected in exclusive populations and other markers distinguished each type (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B.

claims.claim: HC1 and HC3 correspond to Type I HCs and HC2/HC4/HC5 to Type II HCs.
claims.source: Based on prior immunohistochemical analysis (Fischer et al., 2007; Edqvist et al., 2008), we hypothesized that HC1 and HC3 corresponded to Type I and HC2/HC4/HC5 to Type II HCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: HC1 is a mature type and HC3 its immature counterpart.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that HC1 is a mature type and HC3 its immature counterpart.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section as a conclusion from spatiotemporal analysis.

claims.claim: HC2, HC4, and HC5 were distinguished by selective and non-overlapping expression of distinct receptor-type tyrosine kinases, NTRK1, EGFR, and LTK, respectively.
claims.source: The ISL1+LHX1- types HC2, HC4, and HC5 were distinguished by selective and non-overlapping expression of distinct receptor-type tyrosine kinases, NTRK1, EGFR, and LTK, respectively (Figure 4B,D–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B, D-I.

claims.claim: Unsupervised clustering identified 22 groups of BCs ranging in frequency from 1.5 to 10.4% of all BCs.
claims.source: Unsupervised clustering of our data identified 22 groups of BCs (Figure 5A) ranging in frequency from 1.5 to 10.4% of all BCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: All BC clusters expressed the canonical markers VSX2 and OTX2, and each was distinguished by selective expression of other genes.
claims.source: All expressed the canonical markers VSX2 and OTX2, and each was distinguished by selective expression of other genes (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The expression of GRIK1 was mutually exclusive with that of TRPM1 and ISL1 in all BC clusters but one, resulting in 11 likely ON types and 10 likely OFF types.
claims.source: In our dataset, the expression of GRIK1 was mutually exclusive with that of TRPM1 and ISL1 in all clusters but one, resulting in 11 likely ON types and 10 likely OFF types (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claims.claim: PRKCA was expressed at highest levels in BC19, a putative ON cluster, suggesting that it might represent rod BCs.
claims.source: PRKCA was expressed at highest levels in BC19, a putative ON cluster, suggesting that it might represent rod BCs (Greferath et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claims.claim: BC10, which expresses both ON and OFF markers, might have mixed properties.
claims.source: BC10, which expresses both ON and OFF markers might have mixed properties, as has been seen in fish (Yn et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claims.claim: BC1 axons terminated in S3, BC6 and BC8 axons in S3, and BC15 in S4; BC12 axons were bistratified with termini in S1 and S2.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5D–H, BC1 axons terminated in S3, BC6 and BC8 axons in S3, and BC15 in S4; BC12 axons were bistratified with termini in S1 and S2.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5D-H showing eCHIKIN labeling.

claims.claim: Somata of putative OFF (GRIK1+) and ON (TRPM1+) BCs were situated in the outer and inner portions of the INL, respectively, corresponding to the positions of their axon terminals.
claims.source: Somata of putative OFF (GRIK1+) and ON (TRPM1+) BCs were situated in the outer and inner portions of the INL, respectively, corresponding to the positions of their axon terminals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: For most BC types, somata position in INL was correlated with terminal arborization position in IPL.
claims.source: For most types, somata position in INL was correlated with terminal arborization position in IPL (quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 1P, and summarized in Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1P and Figure 5L.

claims.claim: ACs formed the most heterogeneous class in chicks, with 59 putative types ranging in frequency from 0.4 to 7.2% of all ACs.
claims.source: Similarly, ACs formed the most heterogeneous class in chicks, with 59 putative types (Figures 1G and 6A), ranging in frequency from 0.4 to 7.2% of all ACs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figures 1G, 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: All AC clusters expressed SLC32A1, a transporter that loads both GABA and glycine into synaptic vesicles.
claims.source: All expressed SLC32A1, a transporter that loads both GABA and glycine into synaptic vesicles, and each type expressed either GABAergic markers (GABA transporter, SLC6A1, and the GABA synthetic enzymes, GAD1 and GAD2, 40 clusters) or glycinergic markers (glycine transporter 1, SCL6A9, 19 clusters) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6B.

claims.claim: TFAP2A expression was restricted to ACs in the INL, while TFAP2B was expressed by ACs in both INL and GCL.
claims.source: Expression of two broadly expressed member of the AP2 family of transcription factors, TFAP2A and TFAP2B, distinguished these populations: TFAP2A expression was restricted to ACs in the INL, while TFAP2B was expressed by ACs in both locations (Figure 6B,D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6B, D, E.

claims.claim: Two AC clusters, AC7 and AC25, expressed cholinergic markers, indicating their identity as starburst amacrine cells (SACs).
claims.source: Two AC clusters, AC7 and AC25, expressed the cholinergic markers choline acetyltransferase (CHAT), choline transporter (SLC5A7), and vesicular acetylcholine transporter (SLC18A3), indicating their identity as SACs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: AC7 and AC25 are assigned to ON and OFF SACs, respectively.
claims.source: We assign AC7 and AC25 to ON and OFF SACs, respectively, because AC7 expressed FEZF1, a transient marker of developing ON starburst marker in mouse, whereas AC25 expressed TENM3 and ZFHX3, transient OFF markers SAC markers in mouse (Peng et al., 2020; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citation and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: AC37 is the authentic chick VG3 AC, expressing SLC17A8 (VGlut3) and SDK2.
claims.source: AC37 also expressed the recognition molecule Sidekick 2 (SDK2; Yamagata et al., 2002), which is also a selective marker of mouse VG3 ACs (Krishnaswamy et al., 2015; Yamagata and Sanes, 2018), suggesting that AC37 is the authentic chick VG3 AC (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: From 8107 single RGC transcriptomes, 41 clusters were resolved ranging in abundance from 0.6 to 5.1% of all RGCs.
claims.source: From 8107 single RGC transcriptomes, we resolved 41 clusters (Figure 7A) ranging in abundance from 0.6 to 5.1% of all RGCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: All RGC clusters expressed the canonical RGC markers RBPMS and THY1, as well as one or more of the Brn3 (POU4F) transcription factors and the RBPMS homolog, RBPMS2.
claims.source: Like RGCs in mammals, all expressed the canonical RGC markers RBPMS and THY1, as well as one or more of the Brn3 (POU4F) transcription factors and the RBPMS homolog, RBPMS2 (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Cluster 11 selectively expressed OPN4.1 and EOMES, indicating that GC11 is a chick ipRGC type.
claims.source: Among the 41 putative RGC types, cluster 11 selectively expressed OPN4.1, a homolog gene to the defining marker of mammalian intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (ipRGCs), as well as the transcription factor EOMES (Tbr2) (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1I), which is expressed in all but not only ipRGCs (Chaurasia et al., 2005; Mao et al., 2014), indicating that GC11 is a chick ipRGC type.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations and Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: GC25 targets tectal lamina B and GC1 targets tectal lamina F.
claims.source: Based on expression of markers identified in previous studies, we conclude that GC25 targets tectal lamina B (TAC1[substance P]+, NMB [neuromedin B]+, SST [somatostatin I]+, and RELN [reelin]+) and GC1 targets tectal lamina F (CHRNB2 [neuronal acetylcholine receptor beta2 subunit]+, SS2 [somatostatin II], and EZR [ezrin]+) (Yamagata et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claims.claim: Five Müller glia clusters were distinguished in the single-cell dataset of E18 chick retina.
claims.source: However, we distinguished five clusters in the single-cell dataset of E18 chick retina (Figure 8A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: Positional differences underlie Müller glia heterogeneity.
claims.source: This suggested that positional differences might underlie Müller glia heterogeneity.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section as an inference from gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: CHRDL1 (MG1) is selectively expressed in ventral retina, WIF1 (MG2) in dorsal retina, FOXI2 (MG5) in temporal retina, and FOXG1 (BF1) in nasal retina.
claims.source: We documented selective expression of CHRDL1 (MG1) in ventral retina, WIF1 (MG2) in dorsal retina, FOXI2 (MG5) in temporal retina, and FOXG1 (BF1) in nasal retina (Figure 8D–M).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8D-M showing in situ hybridization.

claims.claim: Cells in MG3 cluster were associated with central retina and MG4 with peripheral retina.
claims.source: Finally, in situ hybridization for genes selectively expressed in MG3 (PSCA) and MG4 (TMEM123) indicated that cells in these clusters were associated with central and peripheral retina, respectively (Figure 8N–Q).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8N-Q.

claims.claim: MG3 represents a positionally restricted cell group, whereas MG4 may largely represent immature MGs.
claims.source: Thus, MG3 represents a positionally restricted cell group, whereas MG4 may largely represente immature MGs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section as a conclusion from developmental analysis.

claims.claim: Reclustering of oligodendrocytes revealed five clusters, all expressing the oligodendrocyte marker OLIG2.
claims.source: Reclustering of oligodendrocytes revealed five clusters (Figure 9A; Figure 9—figure supplement 1A). All expressed the oligodendrocyte marker OLIG2 (Zhou et al., 2001), but they exhibited differential expression of other known markers of developing and mature oligodendrocytes (reviewed in Goldman and Kuypers, 2015), suggesting that they represented different developmental stages.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations and Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Pseudotime analysis arranged the oligodendrocyte clusters in the order: OL5, OL3, OL1, OL2, and OL4.
claims.source: Pseudotime analysis arranged the clusters in the order: OL5, OL3, OL1, OL2, and OL4, and selectively expressed markers supported this order.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: PLP1 and BCAS1 were co-expressed in oligodendrocytes, whereas PDGFRA+ cells formed a distinct population.
claims.source: PLP1 and BCAS1 were co-expressed, whereas PDGFRA+ cells formed a distinct population (Figure 9B; Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: BCAS1+PLP1+ oligodendrocytes were more abundant in central retina than in the periphery, whereas PDGFRA+ cells were more abundant peripherally than centrally.
claims.source: BCAS1+PLP1+ cells were more abundant in central retina, near the optic disc, than in the periphery, whereas PDGFRA+ cells were more abundant peripherally than centrally (Figure 9C–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9C-L.

claims.claim: Combining data from chick, mouse, macaque, and human retinal atlases and clustering generated nine clusters, all of which contained cells from all species.
claims.source: To this end, we combined data from the E18/E16 chick atlas with those from our previously published retinal atlases of mouse (Macosko et al., 2015; Shekhar et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2020a), macaque (Peng et al., 2019), and human (Yan et al., 2020b), and submitted the entire group for clustering. This procedure generated nine clusters, all of which contained cells from all species (Figure 10A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations and Figure 10A,B.

claims.claim: Six of the clusters corresponded to major retinal cell classes: rods, cones, HCs, BCs, RGCs, and MG.
claims.source: Six of the clusters corresponded to major retinal cell classes: rods, cones, HCs, BCs, RGCs, and MG.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: The other three clusters were composed of ACs distinguished by neurotransmitter type: GABAergic, glycinergic, and cholinergic+GABAergic (SACs).
claims.source: The other three clusters were composed of ACs distinguished by neurotransmitter type: GABAergic, glycinergic, and cholinergic+GABAergic (SACs); these distinctions are discussed in the next section.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claims.claim: All retinal cell classes remained transcriptomically similar among species and share expression of key genes used to mark each class in mammals.
claims.source: Despite the >300 million years since the mammalian and avian lineages diverged (Kumar and Hedges, 1998), all classes remained transcriptomically similar among species, and share expression of key genes that have been used to mark each class in mammals (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation and Figure 10.

claims.claim: Types within classes are less well conserved than classes themselves across species.
claims.source: In contrast, types within classes are less well conserved: in only a minority cases, such as PRs, SACs, VG3-ACs and ipRGCs, do chick types have orthologous mammalian types as their closest relatives.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The 136 'mature' cell types in the chick atlas are distributed among seven classes: 8 PRs, 4 HCs, 22 BCs, 59 ACs, 41 RGCs, 1 MG, and 1 oligodendrocyte.
claims.source: The 136 'mature' cell types in our atlas are distributed among seven classes: 8 PRs, 4 HCs, 22 BCs, 59 ACs, 41 RGCs, 1 MG (lumping positional variants, as discussed below), and 1 oligodendrocyte.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The number of cell types in the chick atlas is substantially greater than that deduced from morphological surveys.
claims.source: The number is substantially greater than that deduced from morphological surveys (11 BCs, 26 RGCs; Quesada et al., 1988; Naito and Chen, 2004; reviewed in Seifert et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Microglia, astrocytes or diacytes were not detected in the dataset, even though all are known to be present in chick retina.
claims.source: First, we did not detect microglia, astrocytes or a variant glial type named diacytes (Rompani and Cepko, 2010), even though all are known to be present.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claims.claim: The dataset may have been insufficient to detect the least abundant AC and RGC types.
claims.source: Our sample may have been insufficient to detect still less abundant types: they might have been lumped with related types or missed altogether.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claims.claim: The number of AC clusters declined with removal of even 10% of cells, indicating that the dataset was likely too small to capture all types within this class.
claims.source: In contrast, the number of AC clusters declined with removal of even 10% of cells, indicating that our dataset was likely too small to capture all types within this class.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section based on downsampling test results.

claims.claim: The number of cell types in chick is similar to those in mouse, and nearly two-fold higher than those in monkey or human.
claims.source: The number of types in chick is similar to those in mouse, and nearly two-fold higher than those in monkey or human.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section comparing Table 1 data.

claims.claim: The true number of cell types is likely higher in chick than in any mammals sampled to date.
claims.source: Given the sampling limitation discussed above, however, and the larger number of mouse cells profiled (~140,000 vs ~40,000 in chick) we suspect that the true number of types is higher in chick than in any mammals sampled to date.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section as an inference.

claims.claim: An additional 14 clusters represented developmental or positional variants.
claims.source: As noted above, an additional 14 clusters represented developmental or positional variants.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Of 20 eCHIKIN fragments tested, 16 (80%) labeled cells in predicted patterns.
claims.source: Of 20 fragements tested, 16 (80%) labeled cells in predicted patterns, including all cases in which we validated the expression pattern by in situ hybridization or antibodies.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section describing eCHIKIN validation.

claims.claim: To date, only a single Müller glial type has been identified in mice and primates using scRNAseq.
claims.source: To date, only a single Müller glial type has been identified in mice and primates using scRNAseq (Macosko et al., 2015; Shekhar et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Unsupervised analysis of chick Müller glia generated five clusters with a positional basis for the heterogeneity.
claims.source: In contrast, unsupervised analysis of chick Müller glia generated five clusters, which were, however, less well separated from each other than types in other classes. In situ hybridization with probes for genes differentially expressed among these clusters revealed a positional basis for the heterogeneity.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Five of the six Müller glia groups appear to be authentically position-dependent, while the sixth (peripheral) may largely reflect the central-to-peripheral gradient of retinal development.
claims.source: Five of these six groups appear to be authentically position-dependent, based on studies at earlier ages, while the sixth (peripheral) may largely reflect the central-to-peripheral gradient of retinal development that has been observed in several species (Kahn, 1974; Spence and Robson, 1989; Prada et al., 1991; Bruhn and Cepko, 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: 10 clusters fit within cell classes but lacked mature features: four PRs, one HC, one Müller glia, and four oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Although our aim was to profile mature retinal types, we found 10 clusters that fit within cell classes by our criteria, but lacked mature features: four PRrs, one HC, one Müller glia, and four oligodendrocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Several lines of evidence suggested that these 10 clusters were composed of developmental intermediates.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence suggested that these clusters were composed of developmental intermediates.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: All retinal cell classes remained transcriptomically similar among chick, mouse, macaque, and human despite >300 million years since mammalian and avian lineages diverged.
claims.source: The answer to first question is clearly yes. Despite the >300 million years since the mammalian and avian lineages diverged (Kumar and Hedges, 1998), all classes remained transcriptomically similar among species, and share expression of key genes that have been used to mark each class in mammals (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation and Figure 10.

claims.claim: In only a minority of cases do chick types have orthologous mammalian types as their closest relatives.
claims.source: In contrast, types within classes are less well conserved: in only a minority cases, such as PRs, SACs, VG3-ACs and ipRGCs, do chick types have orthologous mammalian types as their closest relatives.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Classes form a common plan within which species evolve distinct types to enable visual behaviors appropriate for their environment.
claims.source: This differences between classes and types supports the idea that classes form a common plan within which species evolve distinct types to enable visual behaviors appropriate for their environment, behavioral repertoire, and other sensory capabilities.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

results.result: The chick retina has a conserved laminar structure with three cellular layers (ONL, INL, GCL) separated by two synaptic layers (OPL, IPL), containing photoreceptors, interneurons (horizontal, bipolar, amacrine cells), Müller glia, retinal ganglion cells, and oligodendrocytes in characteristic positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 describe well-established anatomical features of vertebrate retina that are supported by both the histological image (Figure 1A) and the schematic diagram (Figure 1B). These are foundational anatomical observations consistent with prior knowledge and directly visualized in the provided data.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of E18 chick retina yielded 30,022 high-quality transcriptomes identifying five neuronal classes and two glial types. RGC enrichment using Thy1 antibodies from E16 retina yielded 8,107 RGCs (89% of 9,159 cells), and reclustering generated 150 total clusters representing putative cell types, developmental intermediates, or positional variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 describe the scRNA-seq experimental design and initial clustering results, supported by stated cell counts, figures (1D-H), and methodological details. The interpretation that clusters represent types, intermediates, or variants (C13) is appropriately qualified as presumptive pending further validation.

results.result: The eCHIKIN method was developed for CRISPR-based somatic cell integration of fluorescent reporters into endogenous genes via in ovo electroporation, successfully labeling cell types with 80% efficiency (16/20 fragments) as validated by appropriate cell-type-specific localization of VSX2 (bipolar cells), TFAP2A (amacrine cells), and RBPMS2 (RGCs).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 and C73 describe the eCHIKIN method with clear experimental validation shown in Figure 2. The 80% success rate is explicitly stated with appropriate caveats about validation. The method successfully labels predicted cell types in expected retinal layers, providing strong evidence for its utility.

results.result: Chick photoreceptors comprise tetrachromatic single cones (expressing red, green, blue, or violet opsins), rods (expressing rhodopsin), and double cones (expressing OPN1LW). ScRNA-seq identified 12 PR clusters including 4 single cone types (PR3, 5, 8, 11), 1 rod type (PR3), red single cones (PR7), and three double cone components (PR1, 2, 4).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are supported by prior literature (cited), scRNA-seq data showing opsin expression patterns (Figure 3A-B), and in situ hybridization validation (Figure 3C-G). The identification of PR types based on opsin expression is well-established methodology, and the eCHIKIN labeling of CALB1+ double cones provides morphological confirmation.

results.result: Four PR clusters expressing PRDM1 but lacking opsin expression represent immature photoreceptors. Developmental analysis shows ARHGAP18 is transiently expressed in immature PRs (present at E12, absent at E20), while mature markers like OPN1LW show the opposite pattern, consistent with the known central-to-peripheral gradient of retinal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by gene expression data (PRDM1 expression, lack of opsins), temporal in situ hybridization at E12, E16, and E20 (Figure 3—supplement 2), and consistency with established developmental gradients (cited literature). The inference that these are immature cells is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Five horizontal cell clusters (HC1-5) were identified, all expressing ONECUT3. HC1 and HC3 represent mature and immature Type I HCs (LHX1+/ISL1-), respectively, based on spatiotemporal expression patterns. HC2, HC4, and HC5 represent Type II HCs (ISL1+/LHX1-) distinguished by non-overlapping expression of receptor tyrosine kinases NTRK1, EGFR, and LTK.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by scRNA-seq clustering (Figure 4A-B), marker gene expression validated by in situ hybridization (Figure 4C-L), and spatiotemporal analysis showing OXT (HC3) is peripheral/early and IPCEF1 (HC1) is central/late. The assignment to Type I/II is consistent with prior immunohistochemical studies (cited).

results.result: Twenty-two bipolar cell types were identified, all expressing VSX2 and OTX2. Based on mutually exclusive expression of GRIK1 (OFF) versus TRPM1/ISL1 (ON), 10 OFF and 11 ON types were identified, with BC19 likely representing rod BCs (PRKCA+) and BC10 potentially having mixed ON-OFF properties. eCHIKIN and immunohistochemistry revealed type-specific lamination patterns in the IPL, with soma position in the INL generally correlating with axon terminal position.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 5A-C), eCHIKIN labeling of 5 BC types showing distinct lamination (Figure 5D-H), immunohistochemistry (Figure 5I-K), and quantitative analysis of soma/terminal positions (Figure 5—supplement 1P, Figure 5L). The ON/OFF assignments are appropriately qualified as 'likely' or 'putative' pending physiological confirmation.

results.result: Fifty-nine amacrine cell types were identified, representing the most heterogeneous retinal class. All express SLC32A1, with 40 GABAergic and 19 glycinergic types. TFAP2A distinguishes INL-localized ACs from TFAP2B+ ACs in both layers. Specific types include ON (AC7) and OFF (AC25) starburst ACs identified by differential marker expression, and VG3 glutamatergic ACs (AC37) expressing SLC17A8 and SDK2.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by scRNA-seq clustering (Figure 6A-C), marker gene expression (Figure 6B), immunohistochemistry (Figure 6D-F), and in situ hybridization (Figure 6—supplements). The assignment of SAC subtypes is based on conserved markers from mouse (cited), and the VG3 AC identification is supported by SDK2 expression, a validated marker in mammals.

results.result: Forty-one RGC types were identified from 8,107 transcriptomes, all expressing canonical markers RBPMS, THY1, and POU4F transcription factors. GC11 represents an intrinsically photosensitive RGC type (ipRGC) based on OPN4.1 and EOMES expression. Based on prior marker studies, GC25 projects to tectal lamina B and GC1 to lamina F.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 7A-C), marker gene expression (Figure 7B), in situ hybridization (Figure 7—supplement 1), and eCHIKIN labeling showing morphology (Figure 7F-H). The tectal projection assignments (C50) rely on prior marker studies (cited) rather than direct tracing, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Five Müller glia clusters were distinguished with positional heterogeneity: CHRDL1 (MG1) in ventral, WIF1 (MG2) in dorsal, FOXI2 (MG5) in temporal, FOXG1 in nasal, PSCA (MG3) in central, and TMEM123 (MG4) in peripheral retina. MG3 represents a positionally restricted mature group, while MG4 likely represents immature MGs based on developmental analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by scRNA-seq clustering (Figure 8A-C), extensive in situ hybridization on whole mounts and sections showing position-specific expression (Figure 8D-Q), and developmental analysis at E12 showing TMEM123 is broadly expressed early but becomes peripherally restricted (Figure 8—supplements 2-3). The positional basis is well-documented.

results.result: Five oligodendrocyte clusters were identified, all expressing OLIG2, representing different developmental stages based on differential expression of maturation markers. Pseudotime analysis ordered them as OL5→OL3→OL1→OL2→OL4. Mature BCAS1+/PLP1+ oligodendrocytes are more abundant centrally near the optic disc, while PDGFRA+ precursors are more abundant peripherally.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by scRNA-seq clustering (Figure 9A-B), pseudotime analysis, marker expression consistent with known oligodendrocyte development stages (cited review), and in situ hybridization showing spatial gradients (Figure 9C-L). The developmental interpretation is consistent with known central-to-peripheral oligodendrocyte migration patterns (cited).

results.result: Cross-species analysis combining chick, mouse, macaque, and human retinal atlases generated nine clusters, all containing cells from all species. Six clusters corresponded to major cell classes (rods, cones, HCs, BCs, RGCs, MG), and three to AC subtypes (GABAergic, glycinergic, cholinergic SACs). Despite >300 million years of divergence, all retinal cell classes remained transcriptomically similar across species and share expression of key class-defining genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by integrated clustering analysis (Figure 10A-B), marker gene expression (Figure 10C), and confusion matrix validation (Figure 10D). The finding that all species contribute to all clusters demonstrates class-level conservation. The evolutionary timeframe is appropriately cited (Kumar and Hedges, 1998).

results.result: Cell types within classes are less well conserved across species than the classes themselves. Only in minority cases (PRs, SACs, VG3-ACs, ipRGCs) do chick types have orthologous mammalian types as their closest relatives.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C80 are supported by the dendrogram analyses (Figure 11 and supplements) showing that while classes cluster together across species, most types within classes do not have clear one-to-one orthologs between chick and mammals. The exceptions noted (PRs, SACs, VG3-ACs, ipRGCs) are documented in the figures.

results.result: The chick retinal atlas contains 136 mature cell types (8 PRs, 4 HCs, 22 BCs, 59 ACs, 41 RGCs, 1 MG, 1 oligodendrocyte), substantially more than previous morphological surveys (11 BCs, 26 RGCs). The number is similar to mouse and nearly two-fold higher than macaque or human, though the true number may be higher given sampling limitations and the larger mouse dataset (~140,000 vs ~40,000 cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C70-C71 are supported by the clustering data presented throughout and summarized in Table 1. The comparison to prior morphological studies is appropriately cited. The caveat about potential undersampling (C71) is reasonable given the downsampling analysis (Figure 12) showing AC clusters are not saturated.

results.result: The dataset has limitations: microglia, astrocytes, and diacytes were not detected despite being known to be present. Downsampling analysis indicates the AC dataset was likely too small to capture all types within this class, as cluster number declined with removal of even 10% of cells, unlike BCs and RGCs which were more saturated.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 acknowledge important limitations. C67 is supported by the absence of these cell types in the data and citation of their known presence. C69 is directly supported by the downsampling analysis (Figure 12) showing AC clusters are not saturated, while BC and RGC clusters are stable with 60-80% of cells.

results.result: An additional 14 clusters represented developmental or positional variants rather than mature cell types: four PRs, one HC, one Müller glia, and four oligodendrocytes. Multiple lines of evidence (temporal expression patterns, spatial gradients, E12 profiling, expression of developmental genes) indicate these are developmental intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C77-C78 are supported by the developmental analyses presented for PRs (Figure 3, C24-C27), HCs (Figure 4, C31), Müller glia (Figure 8, C55), and oligodendrocytes (Figure 9, C56-C57). The evidence includes spatiotemporal expression patterns, E12 profiling, and expression of stage-specific markers.

results.result: Unlike mice and primates where only a single Müller glial type has been identified by scRNA-seq, unsupervised analysis of chick Müller glia generated five clusters with positional heterogeneity. Five groups appear authentically position-dependent based on earlier developmental stages, while the sixth (peripheral) may largely reflect the central-to-peripheral developmental gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by comparison to prior mammalian studies (cited), the positional in situ hybridization data (Figure 8), and developmental analysis distinguishing authentic positional identity from developmental gradients (Figure 8—supplements). The distinction between MG3 (positional) and MG4 (developmental) is well-supported by temporal analysis.

results.result: Despite >300 million years since mammalian-avian divergence, all retinal cell classes remained transcriptomically similar among chick, mouse, macaque, and human, sharing expression of key class-defining genes. This supports the idea that classes form a common plan within which species evolve distinct types to enable visual behaviors appropriate for their environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C79 and C81 are supported by the cross-species clustering analysis (Figure 10) showing class-level conservation and the dendrogram analyses (Figure 11) showing type-level divergence. C79 is a data-driven observation, while C81 is an appropriately qualified interpretation ('supports the idea') of the evolutionary pattern observed.

results.result: Hatching (P0) occurs at embryonic day 21 in chicks.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 states a well-established fact about chick development that is consistent with general knowledge and the developmental timeline shown in Figure 1C.
